C-BALANCE-AUDIO-CHANNELS.Summary: Balance the two audio channels against each other and normalise the eight effects among themselves, so an interface sound is actually audible over the ambient music.
C-BALANCE-AUDIO-CHANNELS.Problem: Every click reaches the service — a trace of eleven presses showed the player asked for the effect each time — yet most buttons sound silent to the user, and reproducibly so across restarts. Measured with ffmpeg's volumedetect, the cause is the mix. The ambient bed sits at −27.6 dB effective, while the press effect, taken over its own hundred milliseconds, is at −35.5 dB: eight decibels BELOW the music it plays against, so it is masked throughout its own duration. The other effects fare no better — back is 5.8 dB below, error, open, navigate and close sit within two decibels of the bed — and only toggle (+4.5) and confirm (+6.3) rise above it. Those two are exactly the effects a user hears, and tap with navigate, the two that sit lowest, are exactly the surfaces reported silent: the hub tiles, the cards, the telemetry controls and the header tabs. A second cause compounds the first: the Kenney pack is not loudness-matched, and tap.ogg is inherently 12 dB quieter than the pack's loudest sound, while the per-effect gains shipped (0.7 to 1.0) nudged the levels without ever measuring them. Both mistakes are mine: the channel volumes were chosen by ear against no reference, and the effects were never compared to each other at all.

Goals.Goal: Make the eight effects play at the same loudness, so which effect a surface asks for never decides whether it can be heard.
Give an interface sound a clear margin over the ambient bed, so it reads as a click rather than as a change in the music.
Derive the numbers from measurement rather than taste, and record the measurement so the values are auditable instead of magical.
Pin the mix with a test that fails when the channels or the gains drift apart again, because nothing in the suite could have caught this.
Keep every file's peak below full scale: the fix must not clip a sound that is already peak-normalised.

Constraints.Constraint: Do not re-encode the assets: they are peak-normalised already, and raising them would clip. The balance is achieved by gains and channel volumes.
The player clamps volume to 1.0, so a per-effect gain above 1.0 would be silently capped; the chosen reference level must make every gain at most 1.0.
The interface sounds must not become unpleasant: the reference is the quietest effect, not an arbitrary boost.
Music stays audible as a bed; it is lowered, not silenced.
The ambient rotation, the rotation logic, the fades and the interface-sound debounce are unchanged.

NonGoals.NonGoal: No music ducking on top of the click: that is a larger mechanism and a separate decision, kept out of this change.
No new effects, no re-sourcing of the asset pack, no change to the catalogue.
No user-facing volume sliders: the channels keep their fixed, now measured, levels.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: Every effect's gain is derived from the measured loudness of its file, so the eight land within a decibel and a half of one another, and no gain exceeds 1.0.
The measurement that produced those gains is recorded in the repository alongside the assets, with the command that produced it.
The interface-sound channel's default volume and the music channel's default volume place a click at least eight decibels above the bed.

A test reads the shipped gains and channel volumes and asserts both properties — the eight effects matched, and each comfortably above the music — so a future change to any of those numbers is caught.
The whole suite stays green and flutter analyze reports no new issues on the pinned SDK.

VerificationIntent.ExpectedEvidence: The analyzer reports no new issues and the whole suite passes, including the new mixing test and the existing audio tests. Whether a click now reads clearly over the music can only be judged by listening: the numbers give an eight-decibel margin, and the app running on macOS is how that is confirmed.

Assumptions.Assumption: Mean level over a file's own duration is the right comparison for a short click against a continuous bed; the click's energy in its hundred milliseconds is what competes with the music, not its peak sample.
Eight decibels of margin is enough for a transient click to read over a steady bed; if listening says otherwise the volume is a single constant.
The measured levels of the shipped files stay valid because the files do not change.
